description: roundHalfUp(x) = floor(x + 0.5); a tie always goes to the larger value. Port as floor(x + 0.5) in Kotlin — NOT kotlin.math.round, which breaks ties towards even — and as (x + 0.5).rounded(.down) in Swift. Every weight in the app goes through this.

cases.why: The defining case: 0.5 goes up, not to even.
Ties-to-even agrees here (2), so this case alone cannot detect a wrong port. It is kept so the 1.5 / 2.5 pair shows the divergence side by side.
kotlin.math.round(2.5) returns 2. This is the case that catches a naive Kotlin port.

The tie actually reached in production: describeQuantity(80, portionG 64) computes 80/64 = 1.25, then round1 evaluates roundHalfUp(12.5)/10. Half-up gives "≈ 1,3 portion", ties-to-even gives "≈ 1,2 portion", and nothing reports an error.
Just below the tie rounds down. Brackets the boundary from the left, so an implementation using >= where it should use > is caught.
Just above the tie rounds up. The right-hand bracket of the boundary, so only the exact tie is decided by the tie rule and nothing either side of it is.
An exact integer must not move. floor(n + 0.5) is a common place to introduce an off-by-one when reimplementing.
Zero is reachable (an ingredient scaled down to nothing) and must stay zero.
A real weight computation: 75 g of raw rice at yield 0.85 gives 63.75 g cooked.
A 15 g serving unit halved gives an exact 7.5 g tie, so shortcut increments reach the tie rule as well as portion labels.
